newsitem.title: USA: Blair eyes simpler, more focused 1998 G7.
newsitem.headline: Blair eyes simpler, more focused 1998 G7.

text.p: British Prime Minister Tony Blair, dismayed with the formalities and sprawling communiques he found at his first Group of Seven summit, wants to get back to basics.

Officials said on Sunday that Blair, who will host next year's summit in Birmingham, central England, is determined that it should be a chance for unscripted dialogue on just two main issues -- jobs and the fight against organised crime.

The G7 summit in Denver was the first for Blair, who waselected in a landslide on May 1, and he wants the Birmingham gathering to be less of what one of his senior aides called " a glorified photo call".
"What is important at these summits is that we focus on what we can get done. We must get specifics out of it," Blair told a closing news conference.
The aide said: "There is a need and a desire to get the G7 back much more to what it was at the start."
The New York Times said the annual set pieces bringing together the United States, Japan, Germany, Britain, France Italy and Canada had become "increasingly pompous spectacles of self-promotion".

But French President Jacques Chirac defended the current format. "The fact of being able to discuss all subjects and speak face to face -- that changes everything," he said. British officials said they realised that Blair was not the first leader to try to stem the tide and get back to the "fireside chat" format that then French president Valery Giscard d'Estaing sought for the first economic summit in 1975.
"How many times have we heard that before?" a European diplomat groaned when he heard of Blair's plans.
But British officials said Blair had received a positive feedback to his ideas, which he discussed on the fringes of this weekend's summit, and was determined to produce changes.
One idea is that leaders should head off for a half-day retreat away from the prying eyes of the world's media.

The biennial summit of the Commonwealth, the 54-nation group of Britain and its former colonies, is built round a discreet weekend retreat with minimal contact with the press. Ministers believe the format works well.
G7 "sherpas", the senior officials who prepare the annual summit, will also be instructed to cut down on advance work aimed at agreeing positions on a long laundry list of international issues.
"The prime minister will push for communique-itis to be cured," the senior British official said.
This year's G7 meeting produced two communiques dealing with no fewer than 40 subjects.
"Are they really discussing these in a way that makes a difference?" the official asked rhetorically. "Why don't we have a much more focused debate on the issues?"

The declared intent to put 'employability' at the heart of the Birmingham summit, which will be held from May 15 to 17, 1998, reflects Blair's domestic priority and the main focus of his European diplomacy.

"I believe that by bringing economics back into the economic summit, and at he same time by concentrating on specific issues, we can make a great deal of progress," Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown, Blair's finance minister, said.

He said the Birmingham summit, which will be preceded by a meeting of finance and social affairs ministers in London early next year, would examine policies in six areas crucial to equipping people to adapt to rapid economic change.

These were: modernisation of welfare policies, reform of tax and benefit systems, policies for lifelong learning, measures to nurture small businesses, action to open markets and tackle rigidities impeding business, and steps actively to help those currently shut out of the job market.
"The lesson that I have learned is that it is important to concentrate on quite specific issues and see what progress you can make," Brown said.
